title: Calculus I: Differential and Integral Calculus
description: Limits, derivatives, and integrals as tools for local change and accumulated quantities, with modeling examples from growth, transport, and mechanics.

outcomes.description: Evaluate limits and justify continuity claims.
Use derivatives to analyze and optimize models.
Interpret definite integrals as accumulated change.

lesson_objectives.description: Evaluate limits using algebraic and graphical reasoning.
Use a local linear approximation and estimate its domain of validity.
Differentiate products, quotients, and nested functions.
Keep variables and units attached to a model's rate of change.
Use critical points and endpoints to optimize a continuous model.
Translate geometric or physical constraints before differentiating.
Interpret an integral as signed accumulation.
Use integration to recover a state from its rate.
Relate the specific growth rate r of an exponential model to its derivative and to doubling time, and predict population size at a later time.
Estimate r from two measurements using logarithms and explain why a semi-log plot is linear for exponential growth.
Use the derivative of the logistic model to find the population of maximum growth rate and solve for the time to reach a fraction of capacity.
Evaluate limits of a saturating function at large and small input, and justify continuity and limit claims algebraically.
Use the limit of a difference quotient to find the initial slope of a response and judge the accuracy of the linear approximation near zero.
Interpret a definite integral of a rate as net change, distinguish net change from total change, and evaluate both from a rate function.
Evaluate limits and justify an epsilon–delta criterion.
Distinguish limit values, continuity and one-sided behavior.
Compute derivatives from difference quotients and diagnose corners.
Differentiate products and composite dependencies with units.
Differentiate implicit curves and identify slope validity.
Calculate related rates with multiple changing quantities.
Use derivative signs to analyze extrema and concavity.
Compare feasible stationary points and endpoints.
Eliminate constraints and evaluate model-dependent optima.
Interpret signed sums, definite integrals and accumulated states.
Differentiate accumulation functions with moving bounds.
Apply substitution and calculate average rates.
Compare finite differences and truncation versus noise.
Compute trapezoidal and Simpson quadrature.
Apply error bounds with explicit smoothness and noise assumptions.
Construct local linearizations with curvature error bounds.
Calculate Newton steps and evaluate domain and convergence conditions.
Interpret absolute and dimensionless relative sensitivity.
Estimate exponential rates from dimensionless log ratios.
Calculate how backgrounds and mixed rates alter semilog slopes.
Specify model checks, units and independent validation.
Summarize synthetic observations and calculate endpoint semilog rates.
Compare background correction, half-life and held-out predictions.
Interpret correction uncertainty and limits of model identification.

lessons.title: Limits, continuity, and approximation
lessons.worked_example: For f(x) = x² near x = 3, the linear approximation is f(3+h) ≈ 9 + 6h; at h = 0.1 the approximation is 9.6 versus the exact 9.61.

lessons.title: Derivative rules and chain rule
lessons.worked_example: If response R(c) = 100c/(2+c) and concentration c(t) changes in time, dR/dt = (200/(2+c)²)·dc/dt.

lessons.title: Optimization and related rates
lessons.worked_example: A scaffold design minimizes a cost function over 0 ≤ porosity ≤ 1; an unconstrained stationary point outside that interval is infeasible and must be discarded.

modules.title: Definite integrals and the fundamental theorem

lessons.title: Definite integrals and the fundamental theorem
lessons.worked_example: If a constant infusion adds 2 mg/L per hour for 3 hours with no clearance, concentration rises by 6 mg/L.

modules.title: Derivatives as rates in growth models

lessons.title: Derivatives as rates in growth models: exponential and logistic growth, doubling time and the fastest-growth point
lessons.worked_example: A 24 h doubling time gives r = 0.02888 h⁻¹ and 8×10⁵ cells after 72 h from 10⁵; with K = 10⁶ the logistic rate peaks at 7220 cells/h at K/2, and 90% of K is reached after about 152 h.

lessons.title: Limits of saturating responses and the fundamental theorem as net change
lessons.worked_example: v = 100S/(5 + S) tends to 100 but is 99.50 at S = 1000; its initial slope is 20, and the linear approximation overestimates by 10% at S = 0.5; the rate 6 − 2t gives a net change of 5 mL but 13 mL moved.

modules.title: Limits, continuity and the definition of a derivative

lessons.title: Limits, continuity and the definition of a derivative
lessons.worked_example: Consider H(x) = (x² − 1)/(x − 1) for x ≠ 1, and H(1) = A. Factoring gives H(x) = x + 1 away from the hole, so its limit at 1 is 2. Continuity requires A = 2. With that choice, [H(1+h) − H(1)]/h = [(2+h) − 2]/h = 1 for every nonzero h, hence H′(1) = 1. If A = 5 instead, the quotient is (h − 3)/h and has no finite two-sided limit. Filling the hole incorrectly changes differentiability even though the nearby formula remains the same.

modules.title: Composite functions, implicit curves and related rates

lessons.title: Composite functions, implicit curves and related rates
lessons.worked_example: Use the same response R(c) but let c(t) = 4e^(−0.2t). At t = 0, c = 4 and c′ = −0.8 concentration units per hour. The response slope is 200/(2+4)² = 50/9, so dR/dt = (50/9)(−0.8) = −40/9 = −4.444444 signal units per hour. The negative sign indicates a falling signal. It does not mean a negative concentration or a negative response. The derivative describes local change in a positive quantity.

modules.title: Curve shape, critical points and constrained optimization

lessons.title: Curve shape, critical points and constrained optimization
lessons.worked_example: Suppose the same cylinder must also satisfy h ≤ 1 cm. Since h = 16/r², feasible radii satisfy r ≥ 4 cm. The unconstrained optimum r = 2 is excluded. For r ≥ 4, S′ is positive, so area is minimized at the boundary r = 4, h = 1. Its area is 2π(16) + 2π(4)(1) = 40π cm². The new feasible optimum is larger in area than 24π, because adding a constraint cannot improve the minimum of the same objective over a smaller feasible set.

modules.title: Accumulation, the fundamental theorem and substitution

lessons.title: Accumulation, the fundamental theorem and substitution
lessons.worked_example: Let a synthetic state satisfy x′(t) = 2t/(1+t²), with x(0) = 4. Integrating from 0 to 2 gives the change ln 5, so x(2) = 4 + ln 5 = 5.609438. The average rate is ln 5/2 = 0.804719 over that interval. Differentiating x(t) = 4 + ln(1+t²) recovers the specified rate. Initial state, accumulated change and average rate are three related but distinct quantities.

modules.title: Numerical derivatives, quadrature and error budgets

lessons.title: Numerical derivatives, quadrature and error budgets
lessons.worked_example: Integrate f(t) = t² from 0 to 2 using two panels of width 1. Samples are 0, 1 and 4. Trapezoids give (0/2 + 1 + 4/2) = 3, whereas the exact integral is 8/3. Simpson gives (1/3)(0 + 4×1 + 4) = 8/3 exactly. The fourth derivative of this quadratic is zero, so the Simpson error bound is zero. This exactness for a quadratic does not make Simpson exact for every smooth function.

modules.title: Local approximations, Newton steps and sensitivity

lessons.title: Local approximations, Newton steps and sensitivity
lessons.worked_example: Take f(x) = x² near a = 3. Linearization gives f(3+h) ≈ 9 + 6h, while exact expansion gives 9 + 6h + h². Thus the remainder is exactly h². The curvature bound uses f″ = 2 and gives Mh²/2 = h², equal to the actual error. At h = −0.2, the approximation is 7.8 and the exact value is 7.84. The tangent underestimates on both sides because the function is convex.

modules.title: A washout curve: semilog slopes, background and model checks

lessons.title: A washout curve: semilog slopes, background and model checks
lessons.worked_example: At 0 and 20 h, background-corrected concentrations are 20 and 2.706706. Their ratio gives k = ln(20/2.706706)/20 = 0.1 to the displayed precision. The uncorrected estimate 0.077103 predicts Y(40) ≈ 22e^(−0.077103×40) = 1.006958, while the actual constructed sensor reading is 20e^(−4)+2 = 2.366313. The discrepancy exposes failure of the zero-background model's extrapolation. It does not by itself prove that background is the only possible cause; the known construction supplies that explanation here.

modules.title: Virtual lab 1: washout signals, background and semilog estimates

lessons.title: Virtual lab 1: washout signals, background and semilog estimates
lessons.worked_example: The synthetic raw endpoint signal gives a decay estimate near 0.0771 per hour, while subtraction of the known background gives about 0.1. A zero-background extrapolation underpredicts the reserved late observation; this illustrates model validation rather than identifying a real biological mechanism.

history.summary: Preserved original compact prototype content in separate manifests and readings; labeled partial without semester or credit equivalency.
Added one original quotient-rule item to exercise bounded symbolic-expression grading; the course remains partial.

Added an original lesson on derivatives as rates in exponential and logistic growth models with synthetic data, formative items with computed keys and retrieval cards. The package remains partial and unreviewed.

Added an original lesson on limits of saturating responses, continuity, initial slopes and the fundamental theorem as net change with synthetic data, formative items with computed keys and retrieval cards. The package remains partial and unreviewed.

Assessments with items now also list the course outcomes those items assess, derived from each item's lesson objective and that objective's outcome links. The rubric-only case lists none, and neither do the 4 prototype-unit assessments, whose objectives are not yet linked to an outcome. No readings, items or keys changed. The syllabus was regenerated from the manifest: it states the current version, lists every lesson with its item and card counts, and describes the current practice and limitations (it still described only the four original units). The course limitations shown to learners were also updated: they still described one formative check per lesson and the original numerical rules. The package remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Added seven original lessons on limits and derivative definitions, composite and implicit rates, constrained optimization, accumulation and substitution, numerical calculus and error, local approximations and Newton steps, and the semilog washout case; a synthetic washout-background lab; and a proposed 14-week schedule. Developed with Codex assistance, using existing scope references only. Still partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

limitations: Four compact legacy units remain beside ten original readings, including one synthetic-data virtual lab; this package is not equivalent to a full university semester.
The proposed 14-week schedule is unmeasured and unreviewed. One synthetic lab is not a laboratory sequence; graded homework, exams and an integrative project are not authored.
Formative items and provisional objective associations do not establish comprehensive coverage or mastery.
Bloom labels, prerequisite edges and mathematical accessibility await qualified review.
Answers and feedback are intentionally public practice authoring specifications, not restricted exam keys.
Of the 64 numeric item answers, 9 require a unit; none checks significant figures or dimensions. New bare-number prompts state the relevant output scale. CSV checks use explicit tolerances.
Total and weekly workload are unknown. The proposed schedule is planning scope only.

All new functions, concentrations and observations are synthetic teaching examples. No real clearance rate, biological mechanism, dosing advice, device specification or experimental protocol is established.
intentionally_omitted: Graded assessments, a laboratory sequence, cumulative project, measured workload, accessibility review and qualified human content review remain outstanding.
